prize_parts.citation: for the discovery of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube observatory, opening neutrino astronomy
for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms are interrogated at the magic wavelength, bringing timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B009 for the IceCube discovery and B051 for optical lattice clocks. B009 is still the clearest clue from nature on the table. A diffuse flux of TeV-PeV neutrinos of astrophysical origin was seen in 2013 and has been reproduced in independent analysis channels, and that observation alone, without leaning on the still-developing source associations, opens a new window on where cosmic rays come from. Following Pearce's suggestion, I would now word the citation around the diffuse-flux discovery only. B051 is a different kind of achievement, a measurement capability that reaches new regimes of stability and accuracy. After the first round I am convinced it is a distinct step: Kroll and Lindroth explained that confining thousands of neutral atoms at the magic wavelength, with the trap perturbation cancelled, is a different problem from the single-ion control recognised in 2012 or the comb recognised in 2005. The 10^-18 level has been reproduced in several national laboratories, so the performance is established, and I would not wait for the redefinition of the second, which is a decision for metrologists and not a condition for a discovery prize. Two parts, an observation about the cosmos and a new way to measure time, each stand on their own evidence, and the union is exactly three people.
statement.case_against: The weakest point is the B009 credit. Naming Halzen alone for a collaboration of hundreds, with DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA as precursors, risks misstating how the discovery was made, and Olsson was right to say that a Prize for the original work needs us to be sure we have the right people, not only the project leader. Eva also asks for the person who led the first diffuse-flux analysis, which the credited-name list does not give us. For B051, the objections from Kroll, Johansson and Olsson that Ye's credit may rest on later records and the many-body clock, and that Lemonde and others had early lattice proposals, are not yet answered from the record in front of us. Pearce is also fair that a pairing of unrelated physics can look like a convenience. I accept that, and the defence is that the Prize honours discoveries and not themes, but that defence only holds if each part is individually sound. If the Halzen credit fails the expert check, I would drop B009 and move to B050 instead of widening or inventing a credit.

responses.point: Olsson cannot support B009 because a single credited name for a collaboration of hundreds does not let her say that we identified the people who did the original work, and she asks for expert reports on who conceived the detector and who led the first diffuse-flux analysis.
responses.response: I think that is the right test and I accept it. I do not think the scale of the collaboration is itself disqualifying, since the question is whether the community regards Halzen's conception of the cubic-kilometre detector and his leadership through AMANDA to IceCube as decisive. That is a factual question for outside experts. I would add the diffuse-flux analysis leads to the request, as you say. My position is conditional: if the reports do not support Halzen as the person behind the discovery, I will withdraw B009, and I will not ask the committee to stretch the list of names.

responses.point: Kroll says the lattice clock solves a different problem from Wineland's single ions, namely confining many neutral atoms without first-order perturbation, and that the citation should be drafted narrowly around magic-wavelength lattices so it does not read as a second prize for combs or ion clocks.
responses.response: This moved me further than my eighth-place opening would suggest, and I have taken your drafting advice: the B051 citation now names interrogation of many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength. What I still want from the expert check is the priority record, since your own uncertainty about Lemonde and the early Tokyo and JILA contributions is shared by me. If the record shows Katori as the originator and Ye as the person who delivered the accuracy and many-body clock demonstrations that made the idea a working instrument, I find the two-name credit defensible. If it shows that Ye's role is mainly refinement, I would rather see the committee decide that openly than carry the doubt into the vote.

responses.point: Pearce pushes back on calling the Halzen credit clean and would cite the diffuse flux of 2013 and not the source associations, and he also asks whether a two-part prize with no shared physics is a convenience pairing.
responses.response: I accept the narrowing, and my citation now says diffuse flux. The source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) are significant but still developing, and a prize should not rest on them. On the pairing, I agree it is a convenience unless each part would be defensible alone, so the test I propose is that each half be judged as if it were a one-part prize first. B051 passes that for me on the evidence, while B009 passes only on the attribution check. That keeps the scientific judgement ahead of the arrangement.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B050 as a mature theory-experiment story supplemented by 3D materials and spectroscopy, and would not want it to lose out because of a standoff over a one-laureate collaboration credit.
responses.response: I take that seriously, and it is why B050 remains my first alternative. The science is excellent. My difficulty is the same as yours, which is that the HgTe experiment tested the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and with Zhang's death we cannot recognise the originators of the idea Molenkamp tested, while the 2016 prize covers the same theme. If the expert reports on B009 and the BHZ question both come back unfavourably, I would rather have a B050 prize with an acknowledged weakness than no prize built on a weak credit, and I would then vote for it.

responses.point: Lindroth argues the lattice clock solves how to interrogate many neutral atoms free of Doppler and recoil shifts at once, making 10^-18 stability reachable in hours, and that Ye's Sr clock systematics and Fermi-degenerate many-body clock work are part of the clock achievement itself.
responses.response: That is the clearest statement of why B051 is distinct, and it changed my view of Ye's role: the many-body clock is a real scientific result about interactions in the clock, not just a record. I would use that in the citation language and the committee report. I will not settle the Katori-Ye priority from memory and agree with you that the 2001-2003 papers need checking against the originals before the final ballot.

uncertainties: Whether outside experts support Halzen as the decisive person behind the IceCube diffuse-flux discovery, given the collaboration and the DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA precursors.
Whether the 2001-2003 priority record supports exactly Katori and Ye for the lattice clock, or whether Lemonde or others must be weighed.
Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission and the 2016 prize make B050 workable if B009 fails.
Whether a two-part prize of unrelated physics will be read as a scientific judgement or a convenience.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal to disclose for any shortlisted candidate. My Uppsala position, my supervisor David Gross, and my collaborator Thomas Van Riet are not connected to any credited name. My own work on string-theory dark energy has no link to neutrino astronomy or clock physics. I note the disclosures of Johansson on B038, Pearce on B009 familiarity, and Kroll's distant JILA lineage, and none changes my judgement.
